transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, to be honest with you, doc, I just... I don't feel like myself anymore. Not at all. It's like the battery's been pulled right out of me. I used to be able to at least shoot the breeze, you know? Just regular small talk with the folks who stay late at the offices. But lately, I barely talk to people. I just go completely flat and quiet. It's hard to explain, but it's like my mind just empties out and my face just freezes up, and I don't have the energy to even fake a smile or a nod for the security guards when I clock in. 

And work... I've been a building cleaner for a long time now, took it up after I did a couple years of college back in the day and realized sitting at a desk wasn't for me, but man, these days, just getting started on the cleaning route feels like pushing a loaded cart uphill. I mean a really loaded cart, like when the wheels are locking up on the linoleum and you've got all the heavy trash from the breakroom and you're just dragging it. I'll just stand there in the supply closet staring at the mop bucket, and the thought of just lifting my arm to turn on the faucet feels... impossible. I just don't have whatever it is inside that makes a person go, you know? I just feel blank.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people do not?

Well, it's funny you ask that, doc, because... yes. Actually, yes. And it's been really throwing me off my rhythm, what little rhythm I have left. You see, when I'm doing the late shift, usually after 9 PM when all the accountants and the office folks have gone home, the building gets incredibly quiet. Like, tomb quiet. You can hear the hum of the vending machines all the way down the hall. 

So, I'll be out there with the mop—just doing the main corridor on the third floor, dragging that heavy bucket along—and out of nowhere, I'll hear this voice. It's a man's voice. Deep, kind of gruff, almost like a supervisor from way back. And he'll just say my name. Just clear as day. Or sometimes he'll tell me, "You missed a spot right there." And it sounds exactly like he's standing right by the heavy fire doors near the north stairwell. I mean, it's so real that I'll stop what I'm doing, lean the mop handle against the wall, and walk over to check. I'll even call out, you know, "Hello? Who's down there? Floor is closed." 

But every single time... I look, I push open the door, I check the stairs, I look down the railing, and there is absolutely nobody there. It's just me and the exit sign. And I'll stand there for a good five minutes just trying to figure out how a voice could be so loud and clear when the whole floor is locked down for the night. It really gets to me, because I know I heard it, I know my own ears. I've been working in empty buildings for over twenty years and I know the difference between the pipes settling and a person speaking right next to me, but then the physical space is just... completely empty. And I just have to go back to the mop bucket, but I'm looking over my shoulder the rest of the night.
Have you heard this voice during times when you were not feeling depressed or lacking energy?

Well, now that you mention it... yeah. Yeah, I have. It's not just when I'm feeling like I'm dragging that heavy cart up a hill. There was... I want to say it was a couple months ago, maybe? There was a stretch of time, maybe three, four weeks, where things actually felt a little lighter. I mean, I wouldn't say I was ready to run a marathon or anything, but the fog had kind of lifted a bit. I was actually getting out of bed without staring at the ceiling for an hour first. I was eating regular meals again—you know, actually making a sandwich instead of just eating saltines out of the box because I couldn't be bothered. And work, it wasn't so agonizing. I was just going in, getting the buffing done, emptying the bins, and getting out. I felt almost... normal, I guess you could say. 

But even then, even when I was feeling pretty decent and having an easier time of it... that voice was still there. I'd be feeling fine, humming a little tune maybe, and then—bam—"Hey, you missed a spot," right from the north stairwell. Exactly the same deep, gruff voice. I'd still go check, and there'd still be nobody there. And it wasn't just the voice, either, doc. Even when my mood was up, I couldn't shake this feeling... this absolute certainty that the security cameras in the hallways weren't just there for general building safety. I was convinced—and I mean, I still am, really—that they were being used specifically to track my movements. Like whoever was on the other end of that feed was watching me, waiting for me to mess up, zooming in on me while I worked. So, yeah, even when the depression backed off for a few weeks and I was getting by okay, all that other stuff... the voice in the stairwell, the cameras watching me... it never stopped. It just kept right on going, same as always.
For how long continuously have these experiences occurred while you were not feeling depressed?

Well, like I was saying, it was a solid stretch of time. I’d say it was several weeks, at least. Maybe three or four weeks straight where I was actually feeling pretty decent. The fog had lifted, you know? I wasn't just dragging my feet or staring at the wall. I was getting through my meals—actually sitting down and eating a proper sandwich with some turkey and cheese, maybe a little mustard, instead of just grabbing whatever was easiest and not even tasting it. And work was going smoother, too. I was getting the buffing done, emptying the bins, moving from floor to floor without feeling like I was carrying a hundred-pound weight on my back. I was getting by a little better, feeling almost like my old self for a bit.

But even during those several weeks, even when my mood had lifted some and I was moving around easier... the other stuff didn't go away. Not for a single day. I still heard that gruff voice calling my name down in the north stairwell, clear as a bell, telling me I missed a spot. And I still stayed absolutely convinced that those hallway cameras—the ones with the little red lights that blink every few seconds—were being used to track my every move. I’d be feeling fine, humming a tune, but I’d still be looking up at those lenses, knowing whoever was behind them was zooming in on me. So, yeah, it was a good several weeks where the depression backed off, but the voice and the cameras... they were there the whole time, continuously, right alongside me feeling better.
How long did your most recent period of feeling depressed last continuously?

Well, doc, if I really sit down and map it out... it’s been a long haul. A very long haul. You see, the depression part—that heavy feeling like I'm wearing a lead apron while I'm trying to push my cleaning cart—that's been with me for about a year and two months now. Yeah, one year and two months, almost exactly. 

Because I remember it started not long after the move. And let me tell you, moving at my age, after you've accumulated so much... stuff, so many boxes of old college textbooks I never even use anymore but can't bring myself to throw away, and all my old tools. Packing all that up, getting it into the truck, hauling it to the new place... it just took everything out of me. I thought I was just tired from the physical labor, you know? Just worn out from carrying boxes up and down the stairs. But then the boxes were unpacked, or well, mostly unpacked—there's still a couple sitting in the corner of the living room that I just stare at—and that exhausted, empty, dragging feeling never went away. It just settled right into my bones. 

So from right after that move, fourteen months ago, a year and two months, it’s just been this continuous, unbroken gray cloud. Except for that little three or four-week break I mentioned earlier, of course, where things lifted a bit. But otherwise, the depression part has just been... wading through wet cement every single day. I'd wake up and look at the clock and think about the move and think about the mop bucket and just... yeah, a year and two months.
